title: Ang Thong–Sing Buri 2-Day Trip: Temples, Bang Rachan & River Fish | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A 2-day, 1-night cross-province trip through Ang Thong and Sing Buri, Thailand: the giant Buddha at Wat Muang, the Bang Rachan heroes' park, Luang Pho Phae at Wat Phikun Thong, and riverside Mae La snakehead fish — with real times and routes.
keywords: Ang Thong Sing Buri trip, Ang Thong Sing Buri 2 days, Wat Muang, Bang Rachan camp, Wat Phikun Thong, Mae La snakehead fish
intro: Ang Thong and Sing Buri are two neighboring provinces sitting right on the Asia Highway, about a two-hour drive from Bangkok — perfect for a weekend temple trip you don't have to take days off work for. We've planned the route so day one covers the Ang Thong side, with the giant Buddhas and old temples, and day two crosses over to Sing Buri to follow the Bang Rachan legend before wrapping up with riverside Mae La snakehead fish.

blocks.html: This two-province trip is easy to run because the sights line up along Highway 32 (the Asia Highway) in one long stretch — no doubling back. Day one you drop in on the Ang Thong side, which is known for its huge Buddha images and Ayutthaya-era temples. You can overnight around the town of Ang Thong, or push a bit further and sleep on the Sing Buri side. Day two you follow the history of the Bang Rachan camp, pay respects to Luang Pho Phae, and close out the trip with a riverside fish meal before heading home.

blocks.title: Before you set off
blocks.html: At Wat Phikun Thong (the Luang Pho Phae temple), the museum and some indoor halls mainly open on weekends and public holidays, roughly 09:00–16:30. If you want to see the big image and walk through the full museum, planning your trip on a weekend is the safer bet. The outdoor plaza and the giant image itself are open every day.

blocks.text: Day 1 — The Ang Thong side: giant Buddhas and old temples

blocks.html: The first day focuses on the Ang Thong temple trail, with the highlights being a photogenic giant Buddha and an Ayutthaya-era reclining Buddha. Start a little early and you'll beat both the harsh sun and the crowds.

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Ang Thong — the giant-Buddha merit run

items.activity: Leave Bangkok via Highway 32 (the Asia Highway)
items.note: About a 2-hour drive to Ang Thong. You can stop at a gas station for coffee along the way.

items.activity: Wat Muang, Wiset Chai Chan district — pay respects to the great Buddha, Phra Phuttha Maha Nawamin
items.note: A huge gold seated Buddha in the subduing-Mara posture, rising out of the rice fields — the province's number-one landmark. There's also a heaven-and-hell model zone to walk through. Go early while the sun is still gentle.

items.activity: Wat Khun Inthapramun, Pho Thong district — the great reclining Buddha
items.note: An ancient reclining Buddha about 50 meters long, an open-air image dating back to the Sukhothai–Ayutthaya era. The grounds are open and shaded.

items.activity: Lunch in the town of Ang Thong
items.note: Ang Thong is known for boat noodles and local eats, and there are plenty of spots to choose from in town.

items.activity: Wat Pa Mok Worawihan, Pa Mok district — a reclining Buddha on the Chao Phraya River
items.note: An Ayutthaya-era riverside temple with a beautiful reclining Buddha. This area is also a long-standing home of traditional drum-making — you can stop by the Ekkarat drum-making village.

items.activity: Check in at your accommodation in Ang Thong town and relax
items.note: Take an evening stroll along the Chao Phraya River and find dinner around the town market.

blocks.title: On where to stay
blocks.html: The town of Ang Thong has several budget-friendly hotels and guesthouses, most of them near the Chao Phraya River. If you'd rather wake up and start day two on the Sing Buri side, you can shift over and sleep in the town of Sing Buri instead — it's only about 30–40 minutes away.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Crossing to Sing Buri to follow Bang Rachan

blocks.html: On day two you cross north into Sing Buri. This province is tied to the history of the Bang Rachan heroes, villagers who banded together and held off the army for months — paired with the famous Luang Pho Phae temple and a local specialty: Mae La snakehead fish.

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Sing Buri — history and riverside fish

items.activity: Check out and head into Sing Buri
items.note: Continue north on the Asia Highway, about 30–45 minutes from Ang Thong town.

items.activity: Bang Rachan Heroes' Memorial Park, Khai Bang Rachan district
items.note: There's a monument to the 11 camp leaders, a replica wooden stockade, and a museum that tells the story of the battle. Nearby is Wat Pho Kao Ton, the spiritual center of the Bang Rachan villagers.

items.activity: Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan, Mueang district — one of Thailand's largest reclining Buddhas
items.note: A reclining Buddha over 47 meters long, an Ayutthaya-era image that ranks among the country's biggest. Truly stunning.

A famous provincial spot like Mae La Pla Phao (right on the Asia Highway — look for the giant bottle out front, open daily) serves Mae La snakehead grilled in coconut husk, juicy meat with a punchy dipping sauce.

items.activity: Wat Phikun Thong (the Luang Pho Phae temple), Tha Chang district — pay respects to Phra Phuttha Suwannamongkhon Mahamuni
items.note: A great blessing-posture Buddha beside the Noi River, decorated in gold mosaic, with the Luang Pho Phae museum (the museum mainly opens on weekends).

items.activity: Pick up souvenirs and head back to Bangkok
items.note: Sun-dried snakehead fish and fish sausage are the famous local souvenirs. Leave in the late afternoon and you'll reach Bangkok before dark.

blocks.text: The highlights you shouldn't skip on this route

items.name: Wat Muang — the great Buddha
items.blurb: A huge gold Buddha image rising out of the rice fields in Wiset Chai Chan district, visible from far away — Ang Thong's signature photo spot. There's also a heaven-and-hell model zone around the temple to walk through.
items.meta: Ang Thong · Open daily · Free entry

items.name: Bang Rachan Heroes' Memorial Park
items.blurb: Follow the legend of the Bang Rachan villagers who banded together to fight in the late Ayutthaya period. There's a monument, a replica camp, and a storytelling museum — great for bringing kids to learn some history.

items.name: Wat Phikun Thong (Luang Pho Phae)
items.blurb: A great blessing-posture Buddha beside the Noi River, the temple of Luang Pho Phae, a renowned monk, with a museum keeping his story alive.

items.name: Wat Khun Inthapramun
items.blurb: A large open-air reclining Buddha about 50 meters long, dating back to the Sukhothai era, set in open and shaded grounds in the middle of Ang Thong.

items.name: Wat Phra Non Chaksi Worawihan
items.blurb: A reclining Buddha over 47 meters long, an Ayutthaya-era image that ranks among the largest in Thailand — magnificent and beautifully done.

items.name: Wat Pa Mok Worawihan + drum-making village
items.blurb: An Ayutthaya-era reclining Buddha on the Chao Phraya River. The same area is a long-standing home of traditional drum-making — you can stop in and watch the drum makers at work.

blocks.text: What to eat along the two-province route

blocks.html: The two provinces shine in different ways. Ang Thong is known for boat noodles and local eats, while Sing Buri is river-fish country — especially the Mae La snakehead that grows in the Mae La stream, with firm, sweet meat that's a local specialty drivers passing through tend to stop for.

items: Grilled Mae La snakehead fish — Sing Buri's highlight, grilled in coconut husk so the meat cooks up juicy, dipped in a punchy sauce. Try a famous spot on the Asia Highway like Mae La Pla Phao.
Ang Thong boat noodles — a local favorite in town, chewy noodles in a rich broth. You'll order several bowls a sitting.
Sun-dried snakehead and fish sausage — Sing Buri's go-to souvenir, easy to take home and keeps for a long time.
Local sweets — Ang Thong has Thai desserts and snacks around the town markets; grab a few to take with you before heading back.

blocks.text: Getting around and managing your time smoothly

items.name: Drive yourself
items.blurb: The easiest option for this trip. The sights line up along the Asia Highway in one long run with no backtracking, and every temple has parking.

items.name: Pick your base
items.blurb: Sleep in Ang Thong town the first night, then move up to Sing Buri on day two — or stay in Sing Buri from the start if you want day two close to the sights.

items.name: When to visit
items.blurb: Several temple stops are out in the open, so avoid the midday glare. Start early to cover the outdoor temples first, then save the indoor museums for the afternoon.

blocks.title: Dress for it
blocks.html: Many of the stops are temples, so dress respectfully — sleeved tops and trousers or skirts that cover the knees. Bring an umbrella or hat, since the giant-Buddha plazas are out in the open and the sun is strong, and carry cash for offerings and for buying souvenirs at the markets.

faq.q: How many days is ideal for Ang Thong–Sing Buri?
faq.a: 2 days and 1 night is about right. The first day covers the Ang Thong side (Wat Muang, Wat Khun Inthapramun, Wat Pa Mok) with one overnight, and the second day crosses to Sing Buri to follow the Bang Rachan camp, pay respects to Luang Pho Phae, and eat Mae La snakehead fish. If you're really short on time you could cram it into a single day, but it'll be very rushed.

faq.q: How far apart are the two provinces — is the drive long?
faq.a: Ang Thong and Sing Buri sit right next to each other on Highway 32 (the Asia Highway). From Ang Thong town up to Sing Buri town takes about 30–45 minutes, and from Bangkok to Ang Thong is about 2 hours.

faq.q: Which days is Wat Phikun Thong (Luang Pho Phae) open?
faq.a: The plaza and the outdoor great Buddha are generally open to all. The Luang Pho Phae museum and some indoor areas mainly open on weekends and public holidays that fall on a Saturday or Sunday, roughly 09:00–16:30. If you want to walk through the full museum, planning your trip on a weekend is better.

faq.q: Where's the best place to eat Mae La snakehead fish?
faq.a: A famous spot drivers passing through tend to stop at is Mae La Pla Phao, on the Asia Highway in Sing Buri — look for the giant bottle out front. It's open daily, and the standout dish is Mae La snakehead grilled in coconut husk, with firm, juicy meat.

faq.q: Is this trip suitable for older travelers or kids?
faq.a: It works for both. Most stops are temples and giant Buddha images that older travelers enjoy, while the Bang Rachan camp has a museum and a replica stockade where kids can learn some history. The walking is easy and parking is convenient.
